header: THE HIGH COURT OF SINDH, CIRCUIT COURT AT
Applicant: Mst. Rasheeda through Mr. Haji Khan Jamali,
Respondents No.1&6: Abdul Rehman and Alamghir through
Respondent No.11: The State through Mr. Khalid Hussain Lakho,
body: MUHAMMAD HUMAYON KHAN, J. — The applicant has invoked the jurisdiction of this Court under Section 561-A, Cr.P.C., calling in question the order dated 14.06.2025 passed by the learned Civil Judge and Judicial Magistrate-II, Sakrand, in Crime No.105 of 2024, registered at Police Station Sakrand for offences under Sections 302, 506(2), 337-A(i), 337-F(i), 337-H(ii), 147, 148 and 149, P.P.C. By the impugned order, the learned Magistrate disagreed with the investigating officer’s recommendation to dispose of the case in “C” Class, took cognizance of certain offences, but declined to proceed under Section 302, P.P.C. The applicant seeks interference to that limited extent.

2. The prosecution case, as set out in the FIR, is that the complainant, Mst. Rasheeda, reported an occurrence alleged to have taken place on 29.08.2024. The record states that her statement was recorded at the police station on 27.01.2025 and that FIR No.105 was registered on 28.03.2025. The occurrence is said to have arisen from a longstanding dispute between the parties over landed property. At about 10:00 a.m. on the day in question, the complainant was allegedly present at her house with her sons Muhammad Zaman, Farman and Ali Ghulam when Abdul Rehman, Arif, Shahid, Arbab, Munawar, Alamghir, Aamir, Shubhan, Ayaz and Sodhoro, armed with hatchets, lathis, a sword and pistols, arrived and attacked them. Abdul Rehman allegedly struck Muhammad Zaman on the ear with a hatchet, causing him to fall; Arif allegedly struck him on the head with a lathi. Ayaz allegedly caused a sword injury to Ali Ghulam’s left hand, while Shahid allegedly struck Ali Ghulam on the head with a hatchet. Arbab allegedly caused a lathi injury to Muhammad Irfan’s head. Munawar and Alamghir allegedly resorted to aerial firing, and the accused then left while extending threats. The injured were taken to Taluka Hospital, Sakrand, and Muhammad Zaman was referred for further treatment.

3. The complainant further stated that her son Farman was suffering from kidney disease and was receiving dialysis treatment at SIUT, Karachi. He died there on 20.12.2024. After his funeral, the complainant approached the police and attributed his death to the alleged occurrence.

4. Upon completion of the investigation, the investigating officer submitted a report under Section 173, Cr.P.C., recommending disposal of the case in “C” Class. The officer observed, among other things, that the alleged injuries were not corroborated by the medical evidence in the manner asserted and that no material connected Farman’s death with the occurrence. The learned Magistrate examined the report and the accompanying material, declined the recommendation to dispose of the entire case, and took cognizance under Sections 337-A(i), 337-F(i), 337- L(ii), 148 and 506(2), read with Section 149, P.P.C. He declined to proceed under Section 302, P.P.C. The present application challenges that exclusion.

5. Learned counsel for the applicant contended that the impugned order is contrary to the facts and material on record insofar as it excludes Section 302, P.P.C. He relied upon the allegations in the FIR regarding the accused persons, the weapons allegedly carried by them, the injuries caused to the complainant’s sons and the common object attributed to the group. He submitted that the investigation was not fair and that material witnesses were not examined. He also argued that, despite the complainant’s allegation that Farman’s death resulted from the occurrence, no exhumation or post-mortem examination was arranged to ascertain the cause of death. According to learned counsel, once the Magistrate disagreed with the recommendation for “C” Class, he ought to have proceeded under Section 302, P.P.C., leaving the question of guilt to be decided after evidence. He accordingly sought setting aside of the impugned order to that extent.

6. Learned counsel for respondents No. 1 and 6 supported the impugned order. He submitted that the Magistrate independently considered the police report and the material accompanying it. No specific injury or act of assault upon Farman was attributed to any accused, while the complainant’s own version disclosed that Farman had kidney disease and was undergoing dialysis at SIUT. His death occurred nearly four months after the alleged occurrence, and the available medical record did not connect the death with any assault or injury. It was argued that a bare allegation, without prima facie material linking the occurrence to the death, did not justify proceedings under Section 302, P.P.C.

7. The learned Deputy Prosecutor General, Sindh, submitted that the investigating officer’s opinion under Section 173, Cr.P.C., does not bind the Magistrate, who must independently consider the material under Section 190, Cr.P.C. He further submitted that the allegation under Section 302, P.P.C., must be assessed on the material bearing upon the connection between the alleged acts and the death. He left the matter to the Court.

8. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and the learned Deputy Prosecutor General, Sindh, and have examined the FIR, the report under Section 173, Cr.P.C., the medical documents and the impugned order. The question is whether the learned Magistrate committed an illegality, material irregularity or jurisdictional error in declining to proceed under Section 302, P.P.C., and whether interference is warranted under Section 561-A, Cr.P.C.

9. The opinion of the investigating officer in a report under Section 173, Cr.P.C., is not binding upon the Magistrate. In Muhammad Akbar v. The State (1972 SCMR 335), the Supreme Court held that a Magistrate may take cognizance despite a contrary opinion of the investigating officer where the material before the Magistrate discloses a prima facie case. The Magistrate must therefore apply an independent judicial mind to the police report and the material placed with it.

10. The scope of Section 561-A, Cr.P.C., was considered by the Supreme Court in Aurangzaib Alamgir v. Muhammad Sajid and others (PLD 2025 SC 53). The inherent jurisdiction exists to prevent abuse of the process of a Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. It is not an alternative or additional jurisdiction by which the ordinary procedure may be bypassed. The matter, therefore, is whether the impugned order suffers from a material illegality, jurisdictional defect or miscarriage of justice warranting this Court’s intervention.

11. The impugned order shows that the learned Magistrate did not mechanically accept the investigating officer’s recommendation to dispose of the entire case in “C” Class. He independently considered the material and proceeded in respect of the offences which, in his assessment, were prima facie disclosed. His disagreement with the police recommendation did not require him to proceed under every section mentioned in the FIR. The material supporting cognizance of one offence does not, without more, establish the ingredients of another, particularly an offence alleging that the accused caused a person’s death.

12. The occurrence is alleged to have taken place on 29.08.2024, whereas Farman died on 20.12.2024, approximately three months and twenty-one days later. The FIR attributes particular injuries to Muhammad Zaman, Ali Ghulam and Muhammad Irfan; it does not attribute any specific injury or physical assault to Farman. The complainant’s own account is that Farman was suffering from kidney disease and undergoing dialysis treatment at SIUT, Karachi. The death card records cardiorespiratory arrest. That entry identifies the terminal event; by itself, it does not establish the underlying medical cause or connect the death to the alleged occurrence. No medical opinion or other material has been shown to suggest that the occurrence caused, contributed to or accelerated Farman’s death. On the material presently available, the necessary prima facie link between the alleged acts and the death is absent.

13. The absence of a post-mortem examination is not, in every case, fatal to a prosecution for murder; the cause of death may be established by reliable ocular, medical or circumstantial evidence. Here, however, the record discloses not only the absence of a post-mortem report, but also no specific injury attributed to Farman, his pre-existing illness, the interval between the occurrence and his death, and no other material connecting the two. The failure to arrange an exhumation or post-mortem examination, without supporting material linking the death to the occurrence, cannot by itself supply the factual basis required to proceed under Section 302, P.P.C. Any omission in the investigation may be addressed in accordance with law, but the omission alone does not establish the ingredients of the alleged offence.

14. The submission that the Magistrate was bound to take cognizance under Section 302, P.P.C., merely because he disagreed with the “C” Class recommendation is not well founded. The Magistrate was required to assess the available material independently and could proceed in respect of the offences for which sufficient grounds existed. The impugned order reflects consideration of the relevant material, including the medical record and the circumstances of Farman’s death. The applicant has not identified material demonstrating that the Magistrate overlooked evidence establishing a prima facie connection between the death and the occurrence. The challenge, therefore, discloses no ground for interference under Section 561-A, Cr.P.C.

15. This determination is confined to the legality of the impugned order on the material presently available. It is not a final adjudication of the allegations against the accused. If legally admissible evidence subsequently emerges disclosing an additional offence, the competent Court may exercise the powers available to it under law. The proceedings in respect of the offences already taken cognizance of shall continue independently and in accordance with law, uninfluenced by the observations made in this order.

16. For the foregoing reasons, the applicant has failed to establish any material illegality or jurisdictional infirmity in the impugned order, or prima facie material connecting the occurrence dated 29.08.2024 with Farman’s death on 20.12.2024 so as to warrant proceedings under Section 302, P.P.C. No case for exercise of the inherent jurisdiction of this Court under Section 561-A, Cr.P.C., is made out. The Criminal Miscellaneous Application is dismissed. The order dated 14.06.2025 is maintained to the extent challenged. The learned trial Court shall proceed in accordance with law, uninfluenced by the observations made herein.
